issues.legal_issue: The death of a complainant in a pending criminal complaint does not automatically abate the proceeding, and the complainant’s heirs may be permitted to continue the prosecution.
material_facts: The complainant had filed a criminal complaint, and process had been issued before his death.
After the complainant died, his sons applied to continue the prosecution, and the Magistrate permitted one of them to do so.
The permission order was not challenged, and the criminal proceeding continued with evidence being recorded.
issues.conclusion: The complaint did not abate on the complainant’s death, and the Magistrate could permit a son of the deceased complainant to continue the prosecution.
issues.legal_principle: Section 302 of the Code of Criminal Procedure permits a Magistrate to allow a person to conduct a prosecution; it corresponds to Section 495 of the old Code. In Ashwin Nanubhai Vyas v. State of Maharashtra, the Court held that a complainant’s mother could continue a prosecution after the complainant’s death. Jimmy Jahangir Madan v. Bolly Cariyapa Hindley recognized that a person other than the complainant, including an heir, may seek permission to continue prosecution, although the application there was defective because it was made by power-of-attorney holders. Balasaheb K. Thackeray v. Venkat referred to the same principles without deciding the issue. The criminal complaint here was not subject to a bar like the one considered in Ashwin Nanubhai, and the complainant’s death did not itself terminate the proceeding.

predicates.criminal_complaint_pending_when_complain: A complainant initiated a criminal proceeding that remained pending when the complainant died.
predicates.successor_applies_to_continue: A successor of the deceased complainant applied to continue the prosecution.
predicates.magistrate_permits_successor_to_prosecut: The Magistrate permitted the successor to conduct the prosecution.

issues.definition: When a criminal complaint remains pending at the complainant’s death and a successor applies and receives permission to prosecute, the complaint does not abate and the successor may continue it.

issues.legal_issue: Discretionary appellate intervention is unwarranted where permission for an heir to continue a prosecution became final without challenge and the proceeding continued before a later discharge application was made.
material_facts: The Magistrate permitted a son of the deceased complainant to continue the prosecution, and the accused did not challenge that order.
The prosecution continued and witnesses were examined before the accused applied for discharge.
The discharge application asserted that no prima facie case had been made out; the lower courts rejected it.
The Supreme Court’s notice was confined to whether the complainant’s heirs could continue the complaint.
issues.conclusion: The case was not fit for the Supreme Court to exercise its discretionary power under Article 136 to interfere with the orders below.
issues.legal_principle: Article 136 confers discretionary power on the Supreme Court. The Court declined to exercise that power in light of the unchallenged and final order permitting continuation, the subsequent progress of the prosecution, the timing and limited ground of the discharge application, and the confined scope of the notice in the appeal.

predicates.special_leave_appeal_in_criminal_proceed: An accused brought a criminal-proceeding order before the Supreme Court by special leave appeal.
predicates.successor_permission_order_was_not_chall: The accused did not challenge the order permitting a successor of the deceased complainant to continue the prosecution.
predicates.prosecution_progressed_before_discharge_: The prosecution proceeded and evidence was recorded before the accused applied for discharge.
predicates.discharge_application_relied_only_on_abs: The accused sought discharge on the ground that the material did not establish a prima facie case.

issues.definition: In a criminal special leave appeal, when permission for a successor to prosecute went unchallenged, the prosecution progressed, and a later discharge application relied only on the absence of a prima facie case, the Supreme Court declines discretionary interference.

issues.legal_issue: A pending civil suit concerning the same underlying dispute does not oust the criminal court’s jurisdiction over alleged criminal conduct.
material_facts: A civil suit relating to the dispute was pending while the criminal complaint proceeded.
The complainant’s allegations included cheating and criminal breach of trust.
issues.conclusion: The pending civil suit did not oust the criminal court’s jurisdiction or defeat the criminal proceeding; the civil and criminal proceedings were separate and independent.
issues.legal_principle: Civil and criminal proceedings are separate and independent, and the pendency of a civil suit does not, by itself, oust the jurisdiction of the criminal court where an offence may have been committed. The judgment cites no earlier case or specific statutory provision for this proposition.

predicates.criminal_proceeding_concerns_alleged_cri: A criminal proceeding concerns conduct alleged to constitute an offence.
predicates.civil_suit_concerning_the_dispute_is_pen: A civil suit concerning the same underlying dispute is pending.

issues.definition: When a criminal proceeding concerns alleged criminal conduct and a civil suit concerning the dispute is pending, the civil suit does not oust criminal jurisdiction.
